prompt:
The $n$ players of a hockey team gather to select their team captain. Initially, they stand in a circle, and each person votes for the person on their left.

The players will update their votes via a series of rounds. In one round, each player $a$ updates their vote, one at a time, according to the following procedure: At the time of the update, if $a$ is voting for $b$, and $b$ is voting for $c$, then $a$ updates their vote to $c$. (Note that $a$, $b$, and $c$ need not be distinct; if $b = c$, then $a$'s vote does not change for this update.) Every player updates their vote exactly once in each round, in an order determined by the players (possibly different across different rounds).

They repeat this updating procedure for $n$ rounds. Prove that at this time, all $n$ players will unanimously vote for the same person.
answer: View the votes as a function $f$ (each player points to whom they vote for). The graph always has exactly one cycle; within $\lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor$ rounds the cycle shrinks to a self-loop (it at least halves each round), and then the distances to that player at least halve (rounded up) each round, so $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor + \lceil\log_2(n-1)\rceil \le n$ rounds suffice.

prompt:
Determine all positive integers $a, b, c, p$ where $p$ and $p + 2$ are odd primes and
$$2^a p^b = (p+2)^c - 1.$$

A polynomial $c_dx^d + c_{d-1}x^{d-1} + \cdots + c_1x + c_0$ with degree $d$ is *reflexive* if there is an integer $n \ge d$ such that $c_i = c_{n-i}$ for every $0 \le i \le n$, where $c_i = 0$ for $i > d$. Let $\ell \ge 2$ be an integer and $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Prove that there exist reflexive polynomials $q(x), r(x)$ with integer coefficients such that
$$(1 + x + x^2 + \cdots + x^{\ell-1})\,p(x) = q(x) + x^\ell r(x).$$
answer: With $d = \deg p$, any $m \ge \max(d, 1)$ and $P_m(x) = x^m p(1/x)$, take $q = \dfrac{P_{m+\ell} - p}{x - 1}$ and $r = \dfrac{p - P_m}{x - 1}$; they are integer polynomials, $q + x^\ell r = \dfrac{x^\ell - 1}{x - 1}p$, and $q = x^{m+\ell-1}q(1/x)$, $r = x^{m-1}r(1/x)$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and $AB \ne AC$. Let $D$ and $E$ lie on the arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$ not containing $A$ such that $\angle BAE = \angle DAC$. Let the incenters of $BAE$ and $CAD$ be $X$ and $Y$ respectively, and let the external tangents of the incircles of $BAE$ and $CAD$ intersect at $Z$. Prove that $Z$ lies on the common chord of $\Gamma$ and the circumcircle of $AXY$.
answer: Both $Z$ and the second intersection $N$ of $(AXY)$ with $\Gamma$ lie on the external bisector of $\angle XAY$: for $Z$ because $ZX/ZY = r_X/r_Y = AX/AY$; for $N$ because, with $P, Q$ the second intersections of $AX, AY$ with $\Gamma$, $XP = BP = CQ = YQ$, so $N$ (the spiral-similarity centre taking $XP$ to $YQ$) satisfies $NX = NY$.

solutions.title: External bisector of angle $XAY$
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha = \angle BAE = \angle DAC$, let $r_X, r_Y$ be the inradii of triangles $BAE$ and $CAD$, let the lines $AX$, $AY$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $P$, $Q$, and let the circle $(AXY)$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $N \ne A$; the common chord lies on line $AN$. We show that $Z$ and $N$ both lie on the external bisector of $\angle XAY$.

**Step 1: $Z$ is on the external bisector.** $AX$ bisects $\angle BAE$, so $\angle XAB = \alpha/2$ and $r_X = $ (distance from $X$ to $AB$) $= AX\sin(\alpha/2)$. Likewise $r_Y = AY\sin(\alpha/2)$. Hence $r_X/r_Y = AX/AY$. The intersection $Z$ of the external common tangents is the external centre of similitude of the two incircles: it lies on the line of centres $XY$, outside the segment $XY$, with $ZX/ZY = r_X/r_Y$ (as $Z$ exists, $r_X \ne r_Y$, i.e. $AX \ne AY$). So $ZX/ZY = AX/AY$ with $Z$ outside segment $XY$; by the external angle bisector theorem, the external bisector of $\angle XAY$ meets line $XY$ at exactly this point. So $Z$ lies on the external bisector of $\angle XAY$.

**Step 2: $XP = YQ$.** As $AX$ bisects $\angle BAE$, $P$ is the midpoint of arc $BE$ not containing $A$. Then $PX = PB$ (incenter–excenter lemma): $\angle PBX = \angle PBE + \angle EBX = \angle PAE + \tfrac12\angle ABE = \tfrac12\angle BAE + \tfrac12\angle ABE$, while by the exterior angle of triangle $ABX$, $\angle PXB = \angle XAB + \angle XBA = \tfrac12\angle BAE + \tfrac12\angle ABE$; so triangle $PBX$ is isosceles. In the same way $QY = QC$. Moreover $\angle BAP = \alpha/2 = \angle QAC$, and equal inscribed angles in $\Gamma$ subtend equal chords, so $PB = QC$. Therefore $XP = PB = QC = YQ$.

**Step 3: $N$ is the centre of a rotation taking $X \mapsto Y$, $P\mapsto Q$.** Use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. From the circle $AXYN$: $\measuredangle NXA = \measuredangle NYA$, and since $P \in XA$, $Q \in YA$, this says $\measuredangle NXP = \measuredangle NYQ$. From $\Gamma$ (through $A, P, Q, N$): $\measuredangle NPA = \measuredangle NQA$, i.e. $\measuredangle NPX = \measuredangle NQY$. (The triangles are non-degenerate: line $AP$ meets $\Gamma$ only at $A, P$, and $N \ne P$ because $(AXY)$ meets line $AP$ only at $A$ and $X$.) So triangles $NXP$ and $NYQ$ are directly similar, and since $XP = YQ$ they are directly congruent. Hence $NX = NY$, and the rotation $\rho$ about $N$ with $\rho(X) = Y$ also satisfies $\rho(P) = Q$.

**Step 4: $N$ is on the external bisector.** Let $\theta$ be the angle of $\rho$. Then the vector $\overrightarrow{YQ}$ is $\overrightarrow{XP}$ rotated by $\theta$. Since $X$ lies strictly between $A$ and $P$ (it is inside triangle $ABE$) and $Y$ strictly between $A$ and $Q$, $\overrightarrow{XP}$ points along ray $AX$ and $\overrightarrow{YQ}$ along ray $AY$; so $\theta$ is the signed angle from ray $AX$ to ray $AY$, whose sign is the orientation of triangle $AXY$. But $\theta$ is also the signed angle from $\overrightarrow{NX}$ to $\overrightarrow{NY}$, whose sign is the orientation of triangle $NXY$. So $A$ and $N$ are on the same side of line $XY$: $N$ is on the arc $XY$ of $(AXY)$ that contains $A$, and as $NX = NY$ it is the midpoint of that arc. If $M$ is the midpoint of the other arc $XY$, then $AM$ is the internal bisector of $\angle XAY$ and $MN$ is a diameter (both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $XY$), so $\angle MAN = 90^\circ$: $AN$ is the external bisector of $\angle XAY$.

**Conclusion.** $Z$ and $N$ both lie on the external bisector of $\angle XAY$ through $A$, which is the line $AN$ containing the common chord of $\Gamma$ and $(AXY)$. ∎

prompt:
A rectangle $R$ is divided into a set $S$ of finitely many smaller rectangles with sides parallel to the sides of $R$ such that no three rectangles in $S$ share a common corner. An ant is initially located at the bottom-left corner of $R$. In one operation, we can choose a rectangle $r \in S$ such that the ant is currently located at one of the corners of $r$, say $c$, and move the ant to one of the two corners of $r$ adjacent to $c$.

Suppose that after a finite number of operations, the ant ends up at the top-right corner of $R$. Prove that some rectangle $r \in S$ was chosen in at least two operations.
answer: Even more is true: some rectangle is chosen in two *consecutive* operations. Otherwise every move goes from the bottom-left or top-right corner of the chosen rectangle to its bottom-right or top-left corner (an induction using that no four rectangles meet at a point), so the ant can never arrive at the top-right corner of $R$.

solutions.title: Track which corner of the chosen rectangle the ant uses
solutions.body:
Call the bottom-left and top-right corners of a rectangle its *main* corners and the bottom-right and top-left corners its *side* corners. Each move goes from a corner of the chosen rectangle to an adjacent corner, so it goes from a main corner to a side corner or vice versa. We prove the stronger statement: **if no rectangle is chosen in two consecutive operations, then every move goes from a main corner to a side corner of the chosen rectangle.** This finishes the problem: the last move ends at the top-right corner $T$ of $R$; any rectangle of $S$ having $T$ as a corner lies inside $R$, so $T$ is its top-right corner — a main corner, not a side corner. So some rectangle must be chosen twice in a row, in particular twice.

*Base.* At the start the ant is at the bottom-left corner of $R$, which is the bottom-left (main) corner of the rectangle containing it, so the first move goes main $\to$ side.

*Step.* Suppose a move with rectangle $r$ took the ant from a main corner of $r$ to a side corner $v$, say the bottom-right corner of $r$ (the top-left case is the mirror image). The next rectangle $s \ne r$ has $v$ as a corner. Look at the four quadrants near $v$; $r$ fills the upper-left one.
- $v$ cannot be the bottom-right corner of $s$: then $s$ would also fill the upper-left quadrant near $v$, so $r$ and $s$ would overlap.
- $v$ cannot be the top-left corner of $s$: then $s$ fills the lower-right quadrant. Then $R$ contains points just up-left and just down-right of $v$, hence (being an axis-parallel rectangle) a whole neighbourhood of $v$. The rectangle $t \in S$ covering the points just up-right of $v$ must have $v$ as its bottom-left corner: if $v$ were inside $t$ or on the interior of its bottom or left side, $t$ would also cover points just up-left or just down-right of $v$, overlapping $r$ or $s$. Similarly a rectangle $u$ covering the points just down-left of $v$ has $v$ as its top-right corner. Then $r, s, t, u$ are four rectangles with common corner $v$, contradicting the hypothesis.

So $v$ is the bottom-left or top-right corner of $s$ — a main corner — and the next move goes main $\to$ side. By induction the statement holds for every move. ∎

solutions.title: Arcs and a parity argument
solutions.body:
Suppose every rectangle was chosen at most once. In each rectangle $r \in S$ draw two disjoint arcs inside $r$ joining its corners in pairs: both *horizontal* (bottom-left to bottom-right and top-left to top-right) if the ant moved horizontally using $r$, both *vertical* if it moved vertically, and either choice if $r$ was never used. Every move of the ant runs along one of these arcs, so the ant's journey gives a walk along arcs from the bottom-left corner $A$ of $R$ to its top-right corner $C$.

Consider the graph whose vertices are all corners of rectangles in $S$ and whose edges are the arcs. A corner of $R$ belongs to exactly one rectangle, so it has degree $1$. Any other corner point $v$ is a corner of exactly two rectangles, so it has degree $2$. Indeed, at most two by hypothesis; and if $v$ is a corner of $r$, say $r$ fills the quadrant up-right of $v$, then (as $v$ is not a corner of $R$) the quadrant up-left or the quadrant down-right of $v$ lies in $R$ — say up-left, covered by $t$. If $v$ is not a corner of $t$, then $t$ cannot reach into $r$'s quadrant, so $v$ is inside the right side of $t$ and $t$ also fills the down-left quadrant; then $v$ is not on the bottom edge of $R$, and the rectangle covering the down-right quadrant can overlap neither $r$ nor $t$, so it has $v$ as a corner. (So around $v$ the picture is a T-shape $\vdash, \dashv, \perp, \top$.) A graph with all degrees $1$ or $2$ is a disjoint union of paths and cycles, whose path endpoints are exactly the four corners of $R$. Since $A$ and $C$ are joined by a walk, they are the two ends of one path; so the bottom-right and top-left corners $B$, $D$ of $R$ are the ends of another path. These two paths are disjoint curves inside $R$, one joining the opposite corners $A, C$ and the other joining $B, D$; but such curves must cross (a curve from $A$ to $C$ inside $R$ separates $B$ from $D$). Contradiction. ∎
